name: Cavity Prevention
description: Understand what happens beneath the surface, and give your everyday routine a clear purpose.
keywords: The key takeaway  Early mineral loss can sometimes be reversed. An established cavity needs dental treatment.   What you can do today  Make your technique count:  see brushing and between-teeth guides .     01  How decay starts  Bacteria use sugars and starches to produce acids that remove minerals from enamel. Repeated exposure can lead to a cavity. Early decay may have no symptoms.    02  Early changes vs. a cavity  A white spot can signal early mineral loss. Saliva and fluoride can help repair enamel before a hole forms. Once a cavity develops, a dentist usually restores the damaged tooth with a filling.    03  Your everyday foundations  Brushing matters, but cavity risk also depends on frequency of acidic exposure, diet, saliva, and other individual factors. Fluoride helps enamel resist mineral loss and protective sealants can be placed to protect deep grooves on chewing surfaces. Brush with fluoride toothpaste, clean between teeth, and ask which additional prevention fits your needs.    04  When to book a visit  Pain or sensitivity deserves an assessment; it does not by itself confirm a cavity. Treatment depends on how much of the tooth is affected: a filling may repair a cavity, while deeper damage may require other treatment. For swelling, significant pain, or an injury, contact your dentist promptly.  Read the ADA emergency guide .

name: Gum Health
description: A simple guide to gum inflammation, periodontal disease, and the care that comes next.
keywords: Understand your smile Get to know your gums A simple guide to gum inflammation, periodontal disease, and the care that comes next. Sources checked October 2, 2026 On this page Notice the early signs Gingivitis: inflammation at the gumline Periodontitis: deeper support is affected What your dental team checks Sources The key takeaway Bleeding gums deserve attention. A professional exam can tell you what is happening. What you can do today Notice changes in your gums? Book an assessment rather than trying to diagnose the stage yourself. 01 Notice the early signs Gum inflammation, swelling, tenderness, bleeding, persistent bad breath, or gums pulling away from teeth can signal a problem. Plaque can harden into tartar, which requires professional removal. 02 Gingivitis: inflammation at the gumline Early gum disease can often improve with consistent brushing, cleaning between teeth, and professional care. Ask your dental team to demonstrate a technique that works for you. 03 Periodontitis: deeper support is affected Periodontitis affects the tissues and bone that support teeth. Scaling and root planing, often called periodontal therapy or referred to as a “deep cleaning,” removes deposits below the gumline and cleans affected root surfaces. Treatment and ongoing follow-up aim to control disease; home care remains important. 04 What your dental team checks An examination may include gum-pocket measurements, your medical history, and X-rays to assess bone support. A single measurement alone is not a complete diagnosis. Loose teeth or pain when chewing should be assessed. Sources & further reading NIDCR: Periodontal (gum) disease Educational information to support a conversation with your dental team. Your dentist can assess your individual needs. name: Oral-Systemic Link
description: Oral health is part of whole-person care. Here is how to understand the connections without the alarm.
keywords:
The key takeaway  A link between two conditions does not prove that one causes the other.   What you can do today  Update your medication list and share any health changes with your dental team.     01  What the research tells us  Researchers study links between gum disease and conditions including heart disease and pregnancy complications. Shared risk factors and inflammation may help explain these associations.    02  Diabetes and your mouth  Diabetes increases the likelihood of gum disease and delays healing. Uncontrolled diabetes is highly correlated with more severe periodontal disease, and vice versa. Stabilizing one will often help manage the other.    03  Keep your care team connected  Bring an up-to-date medication list and tell your dental team about health changes, pregnancy, and ongoing treatment.    04  Medications and dry mouth  Some medications can contribute to dry mouth, which raises the risk of decay, gum inflammation, and discomfort. Tell your dental and medical teams about persistent dryness, and discuss medication concerns with the prescriber before changing anything.  Compare dry mouth care formats .  
  Sources & further reading    NIDCR: Healthy mouth, healthy body    NIDCR: Diabetes and oral health    NIDCR: Dry mouth    Educational information to support a conversation with your dental team. Your dentist can assess your individual needs.

name: More than a cleaning
description: Meet the prevention, assessment, and education behind a dental hygienist’s work.
keywords:
The key takeaway  Your hygienist helps you understand your oral health and make a plan for everyday care.   What you can do today  Review your medication list before your next visit.     01  Assess and understand  Hygienists assess oral health, look for signs of disease, take dental X-rays, and share findings with the dentist. They document care so the team can follow changes over time.    02  Clean and protect  Removing plaque, tartar, and stains is part of preventive care. Hygienists may also apply fluoride or sealants to help protect teeth.    03  Make home care practical  Your hygienist focuses on prevention, assessment, and home-care education. The dentist diagnoses conditions and plans restorative treatment; their roles work together. Permitted responsibilities vary by state.    04  Make the most of your visit  A visit may include a health-history update, an examination, a gum assessment, and cleaning. Your dentist recommends X-rays based on your oral health, examination, and individual cavity risk. The recommended frequency may change as your risk changes. Share symptoms, medications, and anything that makes home care difficult. Ask when you should return based on your needs.  
  Sources & further reading    U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Dental hygienists    ADA: What to expect at the dentist    ADA: X-rays    Educational information to support a conversation with your dental team. Your dentist can assess your individual needs.

name: Homecare Routine
description: Daily flossing, brushing, and gum care techniques.
keywords: Good habits, made practical Your daily care, step by step. Floss first, water floss second, use mouthwash third, then brush last. Use fluoride mouthwash for cavity prevention at a separate time of day. Open a card for a quick walkthrough. Maddie’s tip Floss, water floss, mouthwash, then brush. Think of it like sweeping before you mop! The important thing is cleaning between teeth every day and brushing twice a day for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste. A water flosser can be an additional tool for more thorough cleaning beneath the gums. Maddie recommends using a water flosser as additional gum care, alongside daily string flossing—not as a replacement for it. Ask your hygienist how it fits your routine. After brushing, spit out excess toothpaste without rinsing with water or mouthwash, so the fluoride stays on your teeth. 01 / Floss first Flossing basics A gentle curve around each tooth. See the steps + Guide the floss between teeth without snapping it into the gums. Curve it around one tooth in a C shape, then move gently up and down along the side. Clean the neighboring tooth too, and repeat around your mouth, including the backs of the last teeth. Read the ADA guide ↗ 02 / Water floss second Water flossing For more thorough cleaning beneath the gums. See the steps + Maddie recommends using a water flosser as additional gum care, alongside daily string flossing—not as a replacement for it. Follow the setup, tip, and pressure instructions for your particular device. Ask your hygienist to demonstrate the technique for your mouth. Read the ADA guide ↗ 03 / Mouthwash third Mouthwash basics A rinse that fits your needs. See the steps + If using a non-fluoride mouthwash, use it after water flossing and before brushing. Exception: use fluoride mouthwash for cavity prevention at another time of day, such as after lunch, rather than immediately before or after brushing. Follow the product label and your dental team’s directions. Do not swallow mouthwash; follow the label’s waiting period before eating or drinking. Read the NHS guide ↗ 04 / Brush last Brushing basics Two minutes. Twice a day. See the steps + Choose a soft brush and fluoride toothpaste. With a manual brush, angle the bristles toward the gumline at about 45 degrees and use gentle, short strokes. Cover outside, inside, and chewing surfaces. Follow the instructions for your electric brush. Spit out excess toothpaste after brushing. Do not rinse with water or mouthwash: leaving fluoride on your teeth helps protect enamel. Follow your prescriber’s directions for prescription toothpaste. Read the ADA guide ↗ Illustrated learning guides based on American Dental Association and NHS patient resources. Ask your dental team to tailor the technique to you.
